edinburgh.intro_addition: The city's own heritage list adds a yew Robert Louis Stevenson played in as a boy at Colinton, another in the garden of the Hawes Inn, where he wrote part of Kidnapped, and four clipped yews at Malleny that outlived the eight felled beside them in 1961. A redwood in Redford Wood is said to have been planted by a prince of Siam, and a sweet chestnut at Modern One is dated by the gallery it grows beside.
edinburgh.meta_description: Edinburgh's old trees, from Craigmillar's castle yews to the yew Robert Louis Stevenson swung in: 21 trees, their stories and how to reach each.
edinburgh.intro: Edinburgh keeps its oldest trees behind something: a castle wall, a botanic garden fence, the gates of a private estate turned nature reserve, a royal palace's summer-only garden. The city's volcanic crags rarely let a tree grow undisturbed for centuries, so most of what survives does so because an institution built a boundary around it. They range from a pair of castle yews that watched a queen's advisors plot against her husband to the yew Robert Louis Stevenson played in as a boy at Colinton, and four clipped yews at Malleny that outlived the eight felled beside them.

glasgow.intro_addition: Beyond the city, the medieval hunting park at Chatelherault keeps pollarded oaks, one of them dated to around 1440. Motherwell's Dalzell Estate holds a steel-braced oak its council calls probably the oldest living thing in North Lanarkshire, and two yews measured by climbers at nearly 30 metres. At Finlaystone, where admission is charged, a yew tied to John Knox was moved 30 metres around 1900 and survived.
glasgow.meta_description: Glasgow's remarkable trees: the Darnley Sycamore, the Suffragette Oak, Chatelherault's medieval oaks and the Dalzell yews. 10 trees, how to reach each.
glasgow.intro: Glasgow's remarkable trees are civic rather than wild. A 450-year-old sycamore survived a 2025 hurricane, an oak was planted in 1918 as a suffrage protest turned permanent, and an ash on Argyle Street arrived as a seed in holiday primroses. A short trip out, the Wallace Yew stands in Elderslie, the pollarded oaks of Chatelherault's medieval hunting park include one dated to around 1440, and two yews at Motherwell's Dalzell Estate have been measured at nearly 30 metres. Most are free to see; Finlaystone, home of a yew tied to John Knox, charges admission.

wolverhampton.intro: Wolverhampton's oldest trees are churchyard yews on its western edge, and both sets were called ancient long before anyone measured them. In Tettenhall three yews stand in a line on the steep north side of a church that burned in 1950; they were already venerable in 1804, and the biggest is close to seven metres round. In Codsall, a short train ride out, a county historian called the churchyard yews very ancient in 1801. Neither set has been dated, and both are free to visit.
wolverhampton.meta_description: The churchyard yews of Tettenhall and Codsall, called ancient in 1801 and 1804: Wolverhampton's oldest trees, their stories and how to reach them.
wolverhampton.question_meta: Nobody has dated Wolverhampton's oldest trees; the Tettenhall yews, recorded as venerable in 1804 and nearly seven metres round, are the largest.
wolverhampton.question_answer: Nobody has put a reliable age on any of them, so the honest answer is a shortlist. The three yews in Tettenhall churchyard are the largest, the biggest measured at 693 centimetres round in 1999, and they were described as venerable in 1804. The Codsall churchyard yews were called very ancient even earlier, in 1801.
wolverhampton.question_context: Yews are the hardest trees in Britain to date. Their heartwood rots out as they age, which leaves nothing to count, and a girth can only be turned into an age with growth rates that vary wildly from tree to tree. So the evidence for these trees is the written record. In Tettenhall a magazine noted the venerable yews in 1804, the Gardener's Chronicle described all three in 1874 with the bulkiest at 24 feet round, and in 1899 a visiting naturalist declared the great yew more than 2,000 years old, an opinion no modern survey has backed. The church beside them burned in 1950 and was rebuilt around its surviving tower and porch, so the trees are older than most of the building. In Codsall a county historian writing in 1801 called the churchyard yews very ancient and wondered whether they dated from the 13th-century tower. The larger Codsall yew measured 589 centimetres close to the ground in 2003. Both churchyards are open, and the Tettenhall trees, being bigger and better recorded, are the ones we would start with.

faq.q: How big are the Tettenhall yews?
faq.a: The largest, nearest the church, measured 693 centimetres round at a foot off the ground in 1999, and the furthest from the church 681 centimetres at the base. The middle one is a burnt-out hollow shell.
A visitor claimed so for the great Tettenhall yew in 1899, but it was an opinion, not a measurement, and no modern survey supports it. Neither the Tettenhall nor the Codsall yews have a reliable age.

faq.q: Can I visit the yews for free?
faq.a: Yes. Both are in open parish churchyards, St Michael and All Angels in Tettenhall and St Nicholas in Codsall.

faq.q: How do I get to Codsall from Wolverhampton?
faq.a: Codsall has its own station on the railway line from Wolverhampton towards Shrewsbury, and the church is a short walk from the village centre.

cannock-chase.intro: At Shugborough, on the edge of Cannock Chase, a yew that the National Trust calls Europe's widest has spread sideways by rooting its own branches, until its main stem is almost impossible to reach. In Brocton Coppice, the part of Staffordshire with the highest concentration of ancient and veteran trees, walkers have named a gnarled oak after Groot. Neither tree has a reliable age, and only Shugborough charges for entry.
cannock-chase.meta_description: Shugborough's sprawling yew, called Europe's widest, and the Groot oak of Brocton Coppice: Cannock Chase's oldest trees and how to reach them.
cannock-chase.question_meta: Neither of Cannock Chase's best-known old trees has a reliable age; the Groot oak of Brocton Coppice has been guessed at 500 years or more.
cannock-chase.question_answer: Nobody has dated either tree properly. The Groot oak in Brocton Coppice has been guessed at 500 years or more, but only in a photographer's caption. The Great Yew of Shugborough was estimated at 250 to 300 years old in 1898, an estimate we have not been able to check.
cannock-chase.question_context: Brocton Coppice is the stronger answer for the Chase as a whole. It holds the highest concentration of ancient and veteran trees in Staffordshire, old oak woodland among birch, protected as a Site of Special Scientific Interest and a Special Area of Conservation. The oak walkers call Groot is the one with a name, gnarled enough that it earned one, and it has been photographed in 2021, described in 2023 and mapped in 2025. Its age rests on a single guess. Shugborough's yew is better measured but no better dated. In 1898 its crown was given a circumference of 261 feet, by 1992 about 171 metres, because its branches root where they touch the ground and grow on from there. A writer in 1898 thought it 250 to 300 years old, and a later source has suggested a planting around 1700, but we have not seen the evidence for either. The National Trust shows it in the gardens by the Temple, north of the house, with paid entry through the Milford Gates. If you know a better date for either tree, tell us.

faq.q: Is the Shugborough yew really the widest in Europe?
faq.a: The National Trust describes it as Europe's widest yew, and it carries that reputation. No published contest settles it, but its crown was recorded at about 171 metres round in 1992.

faq.q: Why is the Brocton Coppice oak called the Groot Tree?
faq.a: Walkers say its old, gnarled trunk looks like Groot, the walking tree from Guardians of the Galaxy, and it is listed under that name on photo and walking sites.

faq.q: Do I have to pay to see these trees?
faq.a: The Shugborough yew is inside the National Trust estate, which charges for the park and gardens. Brocton Coppice is open woodland and free.

faq.q: Where exactly is the Groot Tree?
faq.a: In Brocton Coppice, reached on foot from the Coppice Hill car park in Brocton. The records of its position differ by some tens of metres, so look for the gnarled oak among the birch.

milton-keynes.intro: Milton Keynes is a new town with old trees inside it. In Great Linford Manor Park a pollarded common lime, dated by one source to the 18th century and by another to 300 to 500 years, has its own boardwalk so visitors stay off its roots. In Howe Park Wood, recorded in the 13th century, local naturalists have named a crab apple Edna and call it the oldest of its kind in the county. Both are free to walk to.
milton-keynes.meta_description: The Linford Lime with its own boardwalk and Edna, the old crab apple of Howe Park Wood: the oldest trees in Milton Keynes and how to find them.
milton-keynes.question_meta: The oldest tree we know in Milton Keynes is the Linford Lime in Great Linford Manor Park, put at anywhere from the 18th century to 500 years old.
milton-keynes.question_answer: The Linford Lime in Great Linford Manor Park is the oldest tree we know of in Milton Keynes. The Parks Trust dates its planting to the 18th century, while a Heritage Open Days listing puts it at 300 to 500 years old, and nobody has published a measurement to settle it.
milton-keynes.question_context: The lime was pollarded long ago, cut back hard so it regrew from a thickened head, which gave it the huge base and wide shape it has now. The Parks Trust, which manages the park, has built a boardwalk underneath it to keep feet off its roots, and a Heritage Open Days event has been held to celebrate it. Its age depends on which source you read. The Trust's notable trees factsheet says it was planted in the 18th century, a photographer's caption calls it part of the park's original 18th-century landscaping, and the Heritage Open Days listing says 300 to 500 years. Without a girth or a ring count, the honest answer is somewhere from about 250 years upward. The other contender is Edna, a crab apple in the north-west corner of Howe Park Wood. Local naturalists call her the finest tree in the wood and think her the oldest of her kind in the county, and a Parks Trust factsheet says well over 100 years. On paper that makes her the younger of the two, and nobody has measured either.

faq.q: Why is there a boardwalk under the Linford Lime?
faq.a: The Parks Trust built it so visitors walk over the tree's roots rather than on them, to protect them for the future.

A crab apple in the north-west corner of Howe Park Wood, named by local naturalists, who call it the finest tree in the wood. It was alive and visited by the Milton Keynes Natural History Society in February 2025.

faq.q: When are the trees at their best?
faq.a: The lime flowers in early summer, when its crown fills with bees. The crab apple blossoms in spring, around late April and May.
Yes. Great Linford Manor Park and Howe Park Wood are both open, free parks managed by The Parks Trust; the wood's paths can be very muddy.
